header: Date: 2026-07-14 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Liang (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Atlas Product), Daniel Lee (Atlas SRE), Omar Haddad (Atlas CTO)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on selecting a primary model for the pilot and defining version pinning + fallback strategy. Redwood presented updated latency/cost tradeoffs across rw-v1, rw-v1-quant, and gpt-4o variants; Atlas emphasized quality failures on long-context receipts and strict 95th pct latency SLO. Agreed next steps include benchmark sheet share, internal evals, and a staged perf run; SE to produce a rollback playbook and recommended pin configs.
topics: Pinning strategies: primary pinned version + fallback variant
Latency vs cost tradeoffs and batching settings
Quality regressions from quantization and long-context behavior
Security/compliance: KMS, audit logs, VPC considerations for Private deployment
transcript:
[00:00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the weekly POC sync. Quick roll call?
[00:00:05] Priya Sharma: Priya here, Daniel, Omar on as well.
[00:00:12] Marcus Liang: Marcus from Redwood, happy to dive into the perf numbers we ran this week.
[00:00:20] Omar Haddad: Great, let's get started, we are short on time.
[00:00:35] Sofia Patel: Okay first slide, Marcus can you summarize the benchmark? We ran the rw-v1 baseline, the rw-v1-quant and gpt-4o small-ish variant on the staging dataset. Latency numbers are medians and 95th.
[00:00:50] Marcus Liang: Sure, so median token latency for rw-v1 was about 18ms per token, 95th at ~120ms. For rw-v1-quant we saw improvements in cost roughly 30% but the 95th tails were a bit twitchy, we see occasional spikes to 220ms under similar batching. gpt-4o small had better hallucination profiles on your docs prompts but cost per token is higher.
[00:01:10] Daniel Lee: When you say spikes, is that due to batching differences or KV cache warmup?
[00:01:20] Marcus Liang: Mostly KV cache warmup and some kernel selection path that isn't as optimal in the quantized execution. We've flagged that as noise but it's repeatable when sequence length goes above ~1k tokens.
[00:01:35] Priya Sharma: Our production traffic has a decent tail for long receipts, yep. We saw more hallucinations on rw-v1-quant on legal text snippets, so that's worrying.
[00:01:45] Marcus Liang: Right, quantization can introduce small numerical shifts, for retrieval-augmented docs it sometimes changes tokens that influence answer derivation.
[00:01:58] Sofia Patel: So recommendation from Redwood for pilot pick? Marcus?
[00:02:05] Marcus Liang: Given your quality constraints and cost goals, we recommend pinning rw-v1 as primary for the pilot and using rw-v1-quant as a fallback for non-sensitive or skip-critical routes. Alternatively a hybrid where we route short-context queries to rw-v1-quant to save cost, and long-context or legal doc routes to rw-v1.
[00:02:26] Omar Haddad: Can you explain pinning and fallback again? We want to avoid surprises when a new model version gets auto-upgraded.
[00:02:35] Marcus Liang: Absolutely. Pinning means you pin a route to a specific model version id, e.g., rw-v1@2026-06-21. Fallback is an ordered list of compatible variants the runtime can route to if primary is unhealthy or overloaded. We support automatic fallback by latency threshold or capacity signals.
[00:02:56] Priya Sharma: How do rollbacks work if we push a change and see a quality regression?
[00:03:05] Marcus Liang: We suggest a canary rollout: pin 5-10% of traffic to the new model, run eval sets and monitors. If quality drops past your regression threshold we rollback by re-pinning to the previous version — it's a single API call or Console button. We also keep trace-level inputs so you can diff outputs.
[00:03:26] Daniel Lee: Is that trace data retained in Hosted mode? For compliance we need audit logs and per-request traces and ability to disable storage for PII.
[00:03:36] Sofia Patel: Good point — Redwood can keep audit logs and you can opt into private retention via Private deployment or configure retention/obfuscation in Dedicated. Marcus, note to include retention options in the security doc.
[00:03:49] Marcus Liang: Will do. Also, for the pilot we can set SLO-based fallback where if 95th latency exceeds 250ms, traffic divert to a lower-cost variant. That avoids errors but can change outputs slightly.
[00:04:05] Priya Sharma: That tradeoff is acceptable for chat summarization but not for legal clause extraction. We need per-route policies.
[00:04:14] Marcus Liang: Yep per-route policies are supported.
[00:04:20] Omar Haddad: About model catalog compatibility — how strict are the fallbacks? Can we fallback from rw-v1 to gpt-4o?
[00:04:30] Marcus Liang: Fallbacks must be compatible by task shape; chat-schema and tokenization differences sometimes mean you need adapter logic. We can fallback to gpt-4o for open-ended generation but for structured extraction you should fallback to variants of the same family.
[00:04:46] Daniel Lee: Any empirical data on hallucination when switching between families mid-session? We worry about inconsistent answers.
[00:04:55] Marcus Liang: We observed some inconsistencies; that's why we recommend per-route pinning and session-affinity during a single conversation. If you must switch mid-session we tag responses and include source metadata so the app can reconcile.
[00:05:12] Priya Sharma: Okay on the pin config, can you propose specific IDs?
[00:05:18] Marcus Liang: Proposed primary: rw-v1@2026-06-21. Fallback: rw-v1-quant@2026-07-02 (for non-sensitive short requests). For experimental long-context improvements we can canary rw-v1-2.1-alpha but that's opt-in.
[00:05:33] Sofia Patel: We'll send that as part of the benchmark doc.
[00:05:40] Priya Sharma: About monitoring: we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route traces. Is that available in your Console?
[00:05:50] Sofia Patel: Yes Console has token-level cost and latency charts, per-model dashboards, and rollout tracing hooks. You can also export metrics to Datadog.
[00:05:59] Daniel Lee: For the perf run you mentioned, what's the approach?
[00:06:05] Marcus Liang: We'll reserve dedicated staging GPUs, replay a sampled traffic distribution (you'll provide), and run at target concurrency to reproduce 95th and P99 tails. We'll test pinned config plus fallback triggers.
[00:06:18] Omar Haddad: Sounds good. Do we need Dedicated or can Hosted handle the pilot?
[00:06:24] Marcus Liang: Hosted works for early pilot; if you need strict isolation or KMS with customer-managed keys we recommend Dedicated or Private. For compliance with higher audit controls you might want Private later.
[00:06:38] Priya Sharma: How about cost modelling — can you show cost delta if we enable automatic fallback to quantized variant for 30% of traffic?
[00:06:46] Marcus Liang: Yes, in the sheet we'll show unit cost and estimated monthly spend for different routing split scenarios. Quick spitball: 30% to rw-v1-quant could drop token spend by ~20% overall but increases risk of regression on certain legal prompts.
[00:07:03] Sofia Patel: Any blockers on your side, Priya?
[00:07:08] Priya Sharma: We need the benchmark sheet and a clear pin/rollback runbook. Also want to ensure the eval set matches our production prompt distribution.
[00:07:16] Marcus Liang: We'll include an eval harness and instructions to run locally; it will attach labels for hallucination, format errors, latency outliers.
[00:07:25] Daniel Lee: Is there a CLI to re-pin quickly in case of incidents?
[00:07:29] Marcus Liang: Yes there's a CLI and an API call to update a route pin; Console also supports revert to previous version. We'll include command examples in the runbook.
[00:07:40] Omar Haddad: Security question, KMS integration for Private — is HSM supported?
[00:07:46] Marcus Liang: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations, and we can provide SOC 2 artifacts for Dedicated.
[00:07:56] Priya Sharma: Great. Any more on model selection?
[00:08:02] Marcus Liang: One more thing — quantized variants can be tuned with per-layer adjustment; sometimes a hybrid quant profile recovers hallucination issues while keeping most cost benefits. It's more engineering effort but possible.
[00:08:18] Priya Sharma: Interesting, would love to see that experiment.
[00:08:22] Sofia Patel: Okay let's recap next steps. Marcus will send the benchmark sheet and runbook, Atlas will run evals and provide traffic sample, and we'll schedule the perf run.
[00:08:34] Marcus Liang: I'll also include the exact pin ids and sample CLI commands.
[00:08:40] Daniel Lee: Thanks all.
[00:08:42] Priya Sharma: Thanks.
[00:08:45] Sofia Patel: Meeting end.
[00:08:48] [00:08:55] Note: transcription may have misspellings — product names sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Dedikated" or similar.
